articles.title: Carnival Orders Two LNG-Powered Cruise Ships from Fincantieri
articles.summary: Italian shipbuilder Fincantieri has signed a contract with Carnival Corporation to design and build two dual-fuel cruise ships for Carnival Cruise Line, with deliveries scheduled for 2033 and 2035.The contract, subject to financing and other customary terms and conditions…
articles.body: Carnival Orders Two LNG-Powered Cruise Ships from Fincantieri Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 20, 2026 © aapsky / Adobe Stock Italian shipbuilder Fincantieri has signed a contract with Carnival Corporation to design and build two dual-fuel cruise ships for Carnival Cruise Line, with deliveries scheduled for 2033 and 2035. The contract, subject to financing and other customary terms and conditions, is classified by Fincantieri as very important, a designation for cruise ship agreements valued at around $2.2 billion (€2 billion). The vessels will be built at Fincantieri's Marghera shipyard and will each have a gross tonnage of approximately 130,000 and around 1,650 guest cabins. Both ships will feature dual-fuel propulsion systems using liquefied natural gas (LNG) as their primary fuel, alongside environmental and digital technologies intended to improve efficiency and reduce emissions. The new vessel design has been developed as a multi-brand platform for Carnival Corporation, with potential for future use across several of its cruise lines. The latest order adds to Fincantieri's existing three-ship Ace-class construction program for Carnival Cruise Line. Construction of the first vessel in that series, Carnival Destiny, began at the shipbuilder's Monfalcone yard in July 2026. Carnival Corporation said it now has 12 new ships on order for delivery through 2039 across Carnival Cruise Line, Princess and AIDA. The agreement extends a 30-year relationship between Fincantieri and Carnival Corporation, during which the shipbuilder has delivered 76 vessels across the group's cruise brands, including 15 for Carnival Cruise Line.

articles.title: GEODIS strengthens Asia Pacific healthcare logistics with GDP certification
articles.summary: GEODIS has announced regional Good Distribution Practices (GDP) certification for its operations across Asia Pacific, strengthening its capabilities in pharmaceutical and healthcare logistics. The certification is based on standards established by the World Health Organization (WHO). It covers certified activities...
articles.body: GEODIS has announced regional Good Distribution Practices (GDP) certification for its operations across Asia Pacific, strengthening its capabilities in pharmaceutical and healthcare logistics. The certification is based on standards established by the World Health Organization (WHO). It covers certified activities involving the handling, storage and distribution of pharmaceutical products, healthcare supplies and medical devices. The development supports GEODIS’ efforts to apply consistent quality procedures across its regional healthcare logistics network. Certification covers temperature-sensitive shipments The certification includes freight forwarding services and temperature-controlled storage, depending on the activities performed at each certified location. The storage requirements cover temperatures of 2–8°C and 15–25°C, supporting the handling of healthcare products with different temperature requirements. GDP standards address several important aspects of pharmaceutical logistics. These include temperature monitoring, documentation, product traceability, risk assessment and staff training. They also establish procedures to help maintain product integrity throughout transportation and storage. According to GEODIS, the regional certification confirms the implementation of quality management systems and controlled operating procedures across the activities covered. The announcement follows the company’s earlier GDP certification for freight forwarding operations in South Korea. By extending its certified capabilities across the region, GEODIS aims to support customers managing complex pharmaceutical supply chains and temperature-sensitive shipments. The company has not specified the number of facilities or countries included in the latest regional certification announcement.

articles.title: Scotland greenlights 1 GW floating offshore wind project
articles.summary: The Scottish Government has granted offshore planning consent for the 1GW Muir Mhòr floating wind farm being developed by Fred. Olsen Seawind off the Aberdeenshire coast. Located approximately 63 km east of Peterhead, the project will comprise up to 67 floating wind turbines capable of generating enough electricity...
articles.body: Europe Offshore Renewables Scotland greenlights 1 GW floating offshore wind project Bojan Lepic November 20, 2026 0 0 1 minute read Ingka Group Ingka Group The Scottish Government has granted offshore planning consent for the 1GW Muir Mhòr floating wind farm being developed by Fred. Olsen Seawind off the Aberdeenshire coast. Located approximately 63 km east of Peterhead, the project will comprise up to 67 floating wind turbines capable of generating enough electricity to meet the equivalent annual consumption of around 1.2m homes. The offshore approval follows onshore planning permission granted last year for the project’s underground cables and substation infrastructure. Muir Mhòr was awarded seabed rights in Scotland’s ScotWind leasing round in 2022 and is among the country’s most advanced commercial-scale floating wind developments. Fred. Olsen Seawind took full ownership of the project earlier this year after acquiring Vattenfall’s 50% interest. The developer is targeting the start of electricity generation in the early 2030s, subject to further commercial and investment decisions. The project has already awarded £18.4m in development contracts, including £7.96m to Scottish suppliers. The latest approval comes with conditions requiring measures to address the wind farm’s potential impact on commercial fisheries and seabirds. The Scottish Fishermen’s Federation criticised the decision, arguing that questions remain about whether fishing vessels can operate safely around the project’s floating foundations, moorings, and subsea cables. Scotland currently has more than 11GW of consented offshore wind capacity, according to the government. The consent is a significant development milestone for Muir Mhòr, although the project has yet to reach a final investment decision. articles.body: Exploration & Production November 20, 2026 · 1 minute ago Türkiye's seismic vessel exploring Pakistan's oil & gas potential in its second overseas mission NS Nadja Skopljak Managing Editor 2 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Oruç Reis. Source: Turkish Ministry of Energy and Natural Resources Türkiye's national seismic research vessel has embarked on its second overseas operation, having arrived in Pakistan where it will be deployed to assess the country's hydrocarbon potential. A welcome ceremony was held today, November 20, at the Port of Karachi where the vessel Oruç Reis has docked, before starting to collect seismic data in the Indus and Makran basins. Within the scope of the Indus-C Block seismic project, Oruç Reis will carry out 3D seismic data collection activities in a 670 km2 area located approximately 120 kilometers off Karachi Port. "Our two nations share common values and deep bonds of brotherhood. The strength of the bond between our countries comes from centuries of shared history and the genuine affection our peoples feel for one another," Turkish Energy and Natural Resources Minister Alparslan Bayraktar said. "We have taken this partnership into the field. We have completed the licensing process for five blocks, three offshore and two onshore, and have begun fieldwork. TPAO will use Oruç Reis to acquire 3D seismic data across 670 square kilometers of the Indus C Block. We expect the survey to take 52 days, or about two months." According to Minister Bayraktar, the aim is to start drilling next year at sites that will be identified by the collected data. "Our work onshore and offshore in Pakistan will directly strengthen the security of energy supply in both countries and contribute to the prosperity of our peoples. We have discovered hydrocarbons and brought them into production in our own waters. We want to achieve the same success in Pakistan," Bayraktar said. articles.title: Sentinel's $2.1B Texas GulfLink Project Faces Regulatory Setback
articles.summary: A court ruling has jeopardized a license for Sentinel Midstream’s $2.1 billion deepwater crude oil export project off the Texas coast, an environmental group that petitioned the court said this week.The ruling, which took effect on October 30…
articles.body: Sentinel's $2.1B Texas GulfLink Project Faces Regulatory Setback Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 20, 2026 (Credit: Sentinel Midstream) A court ruling has jeopardized a license for Sentinel Midstream’s $2.1 billion deepwater crude oil export project off the Texas coast, an environmental group that petitioned the court said this week. The ruling, which took effect on October 30, poses a setback and likely delays for the oil transportation and storage company, which has already started work on the project. It could also impact other pending deepwater port applications. In August, a US appeals court voided a federal record of decision for Sentinel Midstream’s Texas GulfLink project, citing overlap with another deepwater project. An official at Sentinel Midstream said work would continue on the project, characterizing it as "business as usual." But a source with knowledge of the situation said the company could not continue with the offshore project on the current license. Last year, the US Maritime Administration (MARAD), in its record of decision (ROD), approved Texas GulfLink with conditions and the company received its license in January 2026. President Donald Trump has pushed for faster project approvals to bolster the US energy industry. Sentinel made a final investment decision in May and began construction. MARAD's record of decision approving Texas GulfLink's application violated the Deepwater Port Act's requirement that only one deepwater port be approved per application area, the 5th US Circuit Court of Appeals said. Texas GulfLink's application area, when properly designated, would have intersected with Enterprise Products Partners' Sea Port Oil Terminal (SPOT) deepwater project. Congress has struck a careful balance between promoting and regulating the construction and operation of deepwater ports, the court said, holding that the Deepwater Port Act requires an application area to encompass the entirety of a proposed deepwater port site, including any proposed pipeline. “The Court’s decision is clear: it vacated the record of decision that was the foundation of GulfLink’s license. Now, MARAD has to revoke or suspend that license,” Michael Brown, a counsel for the petitioners, said on Wednesday. Construction of the project cannot continue without a federal deepwater port license, said environmental group Better Brazoria Clean Air and Water in a press release this week. MARAD said it was disappointed with the outcome and continues to pursue all avenues to achieve the President’s vision of American energy dominance. "Sentinel is working with MARAD to discuss its options for moving forward. The company cannot continue with the current license," a source familiar with the matter said. In comments to Reuters this week, Sentinel said its license has not been suspended or terminated. Texas GulfLink, to be situated about 30 miles off Freeport, Texas, remains on track for a fourth-quarter 2028 operational date, Bruce Heine, a senior vice president at Sentinel, said this week, adding that given the narrow nature and scope of the issue, there are multiple paths to address the statutory concern without disrupting ongoing construction activities or overall project schedule. "It remains business as usual for Texas GulfLink, with site development and improvement activities currently underway at our Jones Creek onshore terminal facility as we prepare to commence tank construction," Heine said, adding that major long-lead equipment and pipe have been purchased, and key construction contracts executed. However, the company in its motion last month to stay the court mandate said that the Texas GulfLink’s license expressly incorporates the ROD as a compliance standard, adding that voiding the ROD in turn exposed the license to suspension or revocation by MARAD, and prevents construction of offshore components. "At a minimum, the cloud on Texas GulfLink’s regulatory posture will harm Texas GulfLink in the marketplace," the company said then, adding that "given the uncertainty of its ROD and license, Texas GulfLink will not commence construction of the deepwater port under the current posture, even if the mandate is stayed." Texas GulfLink plans to petition the Supreme Court, the company said in its motion. It added that there are two other pending deepwater ports under review with application areas similar to Texas GulfLink’s that will likely require redesignation as a result of the panel’s decision, potentially resulting in consequential impacts to those projects as well. If Sentinel is required to resubmit its application, it would have to await a new ROD and license. While it took nearly seven years for Sentinel to secure approvals last time, MARAD has sped up its approval process under US President Donald Trump. It recently issued a deepwater project application license in just 410 days, nearly 3.7 years faster than the historical average. The Texas GulfLink project aims to fully load a supertanker with about 2 million barrels of oil per day. The administration in recent weeks also approved deepwater port license applications for Energy Transfer's ET.N Blue Marlin Offshore Port, an oil export project off the Louisiana coast, and for ST LNG, which aims to ship liquefied natural gas off the Texas coast. (Reuters - Reporting by Arathy Somasekhar in Houston; additional reporting by David Shepardson; Editing by Liz Hampton and David Gregorio)

articles.title: Cheniere Gets Federal Approval for Major Sabine Pass LNG Expansion
articles.summary: Federal regulators have approved Cheniere Energy's LNG.N application to expand its Sabine Pass liquefied natural gas plant in Louisiana by 20 million metric tons per annum.The three-train expansion project was approved by the Federal Energy…
articles.body: Cheniere Gets Federal Approval for Major Sabine Pass LNG Expansion Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 20, 2026 (Credit: Cheniere) Federal regulators have approved Cheniere Energy's LNG.N application to expand its Sabine Pass liquefied natural gas plant in Louisiana by 20 million metric tons per annum. The three-train expansion project was approved by the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission on Thursday and moves the company one step closer to making a final investment decision for the additional capacity. "This regulatory approval is...a critical milestone on the path toward a positive final investment decision (FID) on the project's first phase, which is expected to add over 6 million tonnes per annum of liquefaction capacity by the early 2030s," Cheniere said in a statement on Thursday. It thanked FERC for the approval and said it comes after a multi-year process. "With commercial support in place, the EPC contract and financing commitments lined up, we are well positioned to reach FID on the first phase of the SPL expansion project in the coming months, after receipt of final regulatory approvals," Cheniere President Zach Davis said on an earnings call earlier this month. Cheniere, the largest LNG exporter in the US, has said it has secured financing for 50% of Phase 1 and has spent about $500 million on early works. The company has been self-financing 50% of its expansion projects and borrowing 50% from banks. Phase 1 of the expansion project is expected to add more than 6 mtpa of capacity and has already been sold on long-term contract. FERC also said it authorized Cheniere to expand the Creole Trail Pipeline Project and Sabine Crossing Pipeline to build and operate a new interstate natural gas pipeline serving the terminal. (Reuters - Reporting by Curtis Williams in Houston; Editing by Nathan Crooks, Nia Williams and Chizu Nomiyama )

articles.title: Europe sends mixed signals on fossil fuels: Norway's climate ruling raises the stakes as EU postpones methane rules
articles.summary: Europe's fossil fuel policy dilemma: Norway’s ruling challenges oil & gas industry over climate impact as EU grants two-year methane reprieve.
articles.body: Authorities & Government November 20, 2026 · 16 minutes ago Europe sends mixed signals on fossil fuels: Norway's climate ruling raises the stakes as EU postpones methane rules Europe's fossil fuel policy dilemma: Norway’s ruling challenges oil & gas industry over climate impact as EU grants two-year methane reprieve. MC Melisa Cavcic Senior Editor 6 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Grane offshore oil platform in the North Sea, which also receives production from the Breidablikk field tied back to it Source: Equinor The growing tension between climate accountability and concerns over energy security and industry competitiveness in Europe is highlighted by two developments, which spotlight two different directions in European fossil fuel policy. Norway's Supreme Court has invalidated approvals for North Sea oil and gas fields over failures to take into account greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions from burning the extracted fuels, strengthening requirements for climate assessments, while the European Union (EU) has agreed to give fossil fuel importers two additional years to comply with methane rules. The Norwegian ruling, which establishes that the climate impact of burning oil and gas needs to be assessed before petroleum projects are approved, declared the approval of plans for the development and operation (PDOs) of offshore fields invalid due to procedural errors. The case concerned the validity of approving PDOs for the Breidablikk and Tyrving fields and the Yggdrasil area, encompassing three fields in the North Sea. According to Supreme Court judgment and order of November 13, 2026, regarding appeal against Borgarting Court of Appeal's judgment and order of November 14, 2025, emissions to air were assessed, but the assessments covered only production emissions and not combustion emissions, so the environmental organizations Föreningen Greenpeace Norden (Greenpeace Nordic) and Young Friends of the Earth Norway (Natur og Ungdom) brought an action seeking declarations that the decisions were invalid due to procedural errors. The Supreme Court sitting as a grand chamber unanimously held that, under the EU Environmental Impact Assessment Directive, as implemented in Norwegian law, the combustion emissions resulting from petroleum extraction must be assessed before a PDO can be approved, which is consistent with the advisory opinion delivered by the European Free Trade Association (EFTA) Court in the case. As the EFTA Court interprets EU law, this requirement applies across the European Economic Area, not just in Norway. The Supreme Court also addressed the extent to which combustion emissions have to be assessed and held by a six-to-five majority that the environmental impact assessment needs to include both the combustion emissions from the project in question and the aggregate emissions from other existing and approved projects on the Norwegian Continental Shelf (NCS), but unanimously agreed that it is not required to address the specific consequences of the increase in temperature that may result from the combustion emissions. Related Articles Fossil Energy North Sea oil project comes on stream ahead of schedule 2 min read The same majority of six justices decided that the environmental impact assessments and the authorities’ evaluations were deficient, as they failed to take into account the aggregate emissions from existing and approved petroleum extraction projects on the NCS; thus, the approvals were declared invalid due to procedural errors. The licence holders were not parties to the case before the Supreme Court. While the fact that the approvals were declared invalid due to procedural errors in proceedings between the environmental organizations and the state does not mean that the licences automatically ceased to have effect vis-à-vis the licence holders, the Norwegian Ministry of Energy has to reconsider the matter on the basis of proper procedure, as the judgment clarifies the requirements applicable to environmental impact assessments of GHG emissions in connection with the approval of PDOs for petroleum deposits. Greenpeace has welcomed the ruling in which the Grand Chamber of Norway’s Supreme Court invalidated permits for three North Sea oil and gas fields, emphasizing that the decision deals “a severe blow” to the Norwegian state and Equinor and Aker BP , which developed the Breidablikk, Yggdrasil, and Tyrving fields. The ruling is a result of a years-long battle for Greenpeace Nordic and Young Friends of the Earth Norway. " This historic ruling changes Norwegian oil policy forever, and sets a precedent the world cannot ignore. Norway can no longer ignore the global damage caused when its oil and gas are burned abroad. Norwegian authorities are now obligated to take into account the enormous climate damage caused by Norwegian oil and gas. This is a momentous victory for global climate justice. " — Haldis Tjeldflaat Helle Norway lead in Greenpeace Nordic Related Articles Fossil Energy Norway greenlights $700 million tie-back project in North Sea 3 min read By affirming lower court rulings, the environmental organization claims that the Supreme Court set a new precedent, establishing that environmental assessments have to evaluate Scope 3 emissions, the carbon released wherever combustion takes place. The case was initiated in 2024. The decision was appealed by the Norwegian government in the Borgarting Court of Appeal and later the Norwegian Supreme Court. " The environmental organizations have won a big victory today, it’s their victory and it’s a privilege to represent them. It’s a huge Grand Chamber win today for the organizations, which will have immense existential repercussions for future generations. Today marks a victory for democracy. " — Attorney Jenny Sandvig of the law firm Simonsen Vogt Wiig, who represents the environmental organizations. In October 2025, the European Court of Human Rights confirmed that Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights requires states to assess the climate impacts of emissions from the burning of fossil fuels, including emissions generated outside their borders, before approving projects. This obligation applies to all Council of Europe members, giving the judgment far-reaching implications for fossil fuel approvals across Europe. Advertisement " This is a huge victory for today’s children who are growing up in a world fundamentally altered by climate change. Young people took the state to court, and we won. It proves that our struggle for climate justice has real force. Now, it is up to the politicians to act. " — Sigrid Hoddevik Losnegård Head of Natur og Ungdom EU delays methane rules by two years after industry pressure Meanwhile, the EU lawmakers and member states have agreed to postpone key methane requirements for fossil fuel imports until 2029, raising concerns among environmental organizations about the strength of the bloc's climate commitments. The Council of the European Union and the European Parliament reached a provisional agreement on targeted amendments to the EU methane regulation on November 19, 2026, securing a two-year postponement for the application of specific methane-related monitoring, reporting and verification obligations applicable to imports of crude oil, natural gas and coal. The move is said to provide flexibility for operators and member states to safeguard reliable and secure energy supplies amid global volatility, while upholding the EU’s commitment to reducing methane emissions in line with its climate ambitions, after EU leaders welcomed the European Commission's proposal to postpone certain obligations in the methane regulation to address the impact of the current geopolitical context on global supply chains, energy security, and energy and fuel prices. The co-legislators agreed that additional time is needed for third countries, member states, producers, importers, operators and traders to comply fully with the methane regulation, allowing them to develop the necessary implementation tools. As a result, the application of monitoring, reporting and verification obligations for natural gas, crude oil and coal importers will apply from January 1, 2029, instead of January 1, 2027, while methane-intensity reporting for both importers and EU producers will apply from August 5, 2030, instead of August 5, 2028. " Tonight, we achieved a pragmatic balance on the methane regulation, addressing the pressures in the energy market while maintaining the EU’s leadership in reducing methane emissions. This provisional agreement demonstrates the EU’s commitment to an effective approach to cutting harmful methane emissions while shielding our citizens from high energy prices. " — Darragh O’Brien Ireland’s Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment Related Articles Fossil Energy EU’s first-ever methane clampdown regulation becoming law of the land 4 min read Building on the European Council’s negotiating mandate, the co-legislators agreed that the Commission will review the effective implementation of the methane regulation by January 1, 2028, in establishing transparent and accurate measurement, reporting and verification rules and reducing methane emissions from imported fossil fuels. The review will include the availability of a sufficient number of third-party verifiers to assess the conformity of the emission reports and any potential implications for the security of supply. The provisional agreement will now have to be endorsed by the European Council and the Parliament. Afterward, the targeted amendment to the methane regulation will be formally adopted by both institutions and enter into force before the end of the year. Since methane is a powerful greenhouse gas, it is estimated to be responsible for approximately 30% of global warming, which makes its reduction crucial for achieving the EU’s climate objectives. While commenting on this decision, the Greens/EFA in the European Parliament said the EU had caved in to the fossil fuel lobby, since a majority of center-right to far-right MEPs agreed to postpone the implementation of certain parts of the methane regulation by two years even though methane emissions are responsible for about a third of global warming, with the energy sector alone accounting for 10% of the global rise in temperature. " The EU is caving in to the fossil fuel lobby and the Trump administration. While the European Commission and EU member states are pushing to include a commitment to reduce methane emissions in the final text of the global climate conference in Antalya, they are simultaneously kicking the implementation of a key instrument for achieving this down the road in Brussels. It is impossible to justify how the wasteful flaring and venting of gas should somehow enhance energy security or reduce bills for consumers, especially at a time of tight supplies and high prices. " — Jutta Paulus Greens/EFA member and former European Parliament’s lead negotiator for the methane regulation Related Articles Fossil Energy €4.5 trillion investor coalition urges EU to hold the line on methane cuts 4 min read Clean Air Taskforce emphasized that the provisional deal to delay key provisions of the EU methane regulation should not become a pause on progress. " A two-year delay doesn’t have a technical justification. Costs and security of supply were overblown arguments from the beginning, and the issues around verification and certification can be solved within the first year. Details of the deal are still emerging, and while a worst-case scenario seems to have been avoided, these delays affect the credibility of the EU legislation and deal a hard blow to the hopes of fast methane emission reductions that are our best hope to limit global warming in the short term. It is now up to the Commission and Member States to advance on implementation to ensure this delay doesn’t become a pause on progress. " — Pablo Lopez Legarreta Europe Policy Manager for Methane Pollution Prevention at CATF While the Norwegian case concerns the adequacy of environmental impact assessments, particularly the assessment of greenhouse gas emissions resulting from the eventual combustion of extracted oil and gas, the EU's methane rules address methane emissions across the fossil fuel supply chain, including production, processing, transport, and imports. Although these developments concern distinct legal and regulatory issues, both raise questions about the responsibility of the fossil fuel industry for the climate impacts associated with the extraction and supply of fossil fuels, illustrating the tensions within European climate and energy governance. While legal and regulatory frameworks increasingly seek to strengthen the accountability of fossil fuel producers and importers for their emissions, these efforts need to also be reconciled with concerns about energy security and affordability. These contrasting developments serve to emphasize the EU's broader challenge of balancing the competing objectives of the energy trilemma by finding ways to come to grips with energy security, affordability, and environmental sustainability. articles.body: Oil Prices Rise as Houthi Strikes Revive Supply Disruption Fears Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 20, 2026 © Pixim Stock / Adobe Stock Oil prices rose on Friday but were set for a weekly decline as concerns over supply disruptions grew following Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia's capital Riyadh and reports of tanker disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz. Brent crude futures LCOc1 rose 59 cents, or 0.6%, to $92.57 a barrel by 0720 GMT. US West Texas Intermediate futures for December CLc1 climbed 42 cents, or 0.5%, to $83.63 a barrel, while the more-active January contract CLc2 gained 60 cents, or 0.7%, to $83.04. Both benchmarks were little changed on Thursday, but Brent is set for a 3.5% decline for the week and the December WTI contract for an almost 6% weekly drop as expectations of a supply surplus grew because crude shipments through the Strait of Hormuz have returned to roughly prewar levels. This will be the benchmarks' third straight week of decline. "Concerns over Middle Eastern crude oil supplies have resurfaced due to attacks on Riyadh by the Houthis, prompting buying," said Satoru Yoshida, a commodity analyst with Rakuten Securities. "Expectations that coordinated production cuts will continue at the OPEC+ meeting later this month are also providing support," he said. The Iran-aligned Houthi movement fired missiles at Riyadh, the latest blow to the kingdom in its war with the Houthis. Two oil tankers also hit naval mines in the Strait of Hormuz and "exploded" and "are burning", Iran's Revolutionary Guards Navy said in a statement carried by state media on Thursday. Iran's intensifying attacks on tankers transiting the Strait of Hormuz, "running at roughly one incident per day in November", still add a meaningful geopolitical risk premium to the market, according to UOB Group analysts in a client note. OPEC+ ministers will hold a series of meetings on November 29 to decide their 2027 output policy. The group comprises the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries and allies such as Russia. The Middle East conflict has caused the biggest disruption ever to global oil and gas trade and could cut world oil demand by more than 4% by 2035 if governments accelerate electrification, efficiency and fuel-switching measures in response, the International Energy Agency said on Thursday. However, some analysts were still expecting softness in the broader equities markets to weigh on oil prices, as Asian shares fell on Friday — heading for their worst week since 2020. Ukrainian drone attacks have slashed Russian oil refineries' combined crude processing volumes by 45% since late October, Reuters reported on Wednesday. articles.body: PSA Singapore has started construction of the second phase of Tuas Port, marking a major milestone in the expansion of Singapore’s container port infrastructure. The development will add 21 mega berths and 8.6 kilometres of wharf. The new berths will have a water depth of 23 metres, allowing them to accommodate the world’s largest container vessels. Phase Two is the largest of Tuas Port’s four development phases in terms of wharf length. Operations are expected to begin gradually from 2028. The expansion aims to strengthen Singapore’s position as a global container transshipment hub and support growing demand for efficient cargo handling. Automation to play a central role PSA plans to expand the use of automation and artificial intelligence across the new terminal facilities. Once Phase Two is completed, nearly 1,000 autonomous Intelligent Guided Vehicles (IGVs) will move containers around the terminal. These AI-enabled vehicles will help coordinate container movements and improve the efficiency of daily port operations. The new facilities will also connect with PSA’s wider digital systems and the PSA Supply Chain Hub @ Tuas. This will support better coordination between terminal activities and inland logistics. “Global trade continues to evolve amid shifting supply chains and changing market dynamics,” said Peter Voser, Group Chairman, PSA International. “PSA must continue to invest in the capabilities and connectivity needed to remain relevant and create value for decades to come,” Voser added. Meanwhile, PSA Group CEO Ong Kim Pong highlighted the importance of combining new infrastructure with advanced technology. He said the development would support more coordinated terminal operations and strengthen connections across the wider supply chain. The project forms part of Tuas Port’s long-term development, following the start of operations in September 2022. PSA Singapore handled 44.5 million TEUs across its Singapore terminals in 2025. The company did not disclose the investment value of Phase Two in its latest announcement.

articles.title: From Fragmented Plans to Superintelligent Terminals

articles.body: Container terminals face growing pressure to move more cargo, turn vessels around faster and control costs within existing infrastructure. Yet even terminals with sophisticated planning tools can struggle when berth scheduling, vessel stowage, yard allocation and equipment dispatch operate independently. A plan that works for one department may create congestion, delays or unnecessary moves elsewhere. The opportunity lies in connecting these decisions through integrated, AI-driven planning, clear visualisation and turning operational information into actionable knowledge. Turning information into knowledge Information alone does not create understanding. Terminal teams receive vast amounts of operational data, but people cannot retain every event or interpret every interaction. We cannot learn from what we cannot see. As events disappear from view and memories fade, investigations often depend on fragmented observations, reports and recollections. TOPX Intelligent 3D helps bridge this gap. Much more than just a digital twin, it combines a live 3D operational environment with planning and execution capabilities, connecting teams to see decisions they can act upon. Historical playback helps operators revisit events and establish what happened. X-ray visualization reveals operational details that may otherwise remain obscured. Near-future simulation helps teams examine developing conditions and assess responses before disruption escalates. Together, these capabilities support a clearer understanding of what happened, why it happened and how to address it. From reactive control to predictive performance The SuperIntelligent capabilities of TOPX Intelligent 3D bring past events, current operations and anticipated conditions into one decision-making environment. AI-driven analysis helps identify emerging delays, congestion and resource conflicts, supporting earlier intervention and coordinated responses. This shifts terminal management from memory-based judgement towards decisions grounded in recorded facts and clear visualization. Planners retain operational oversight while gaining a broader view of consequences across berth, vessel, yard and equipment activities. For terminal operators, port authorities and shipping companies, the goal is practical: more predictable vessel calls, more productive assets and greater throughput. Integrated planning and a superintelligent digital twin provide a pathway from fragmented decisions to continuous, terminal-wide improvement. Connecting every planning decision RBS’s High Precision Planning brings berth planning, Automatic Vessel Planning (AVP), yard planning and equipment optimization into a continuous planning and execution cycle. Rather than treating each function as a separate task, it considers how decisions affect performance across the terminal. Through TOPX Expert, AVP helps align vessel loading sequences with yard availability and equipment resources. Real-time operational updates allow plans to adapt as conditions change, helping reduce crane waiting, avoid conflicting equipment demands and maintain a more consistent flow of containers. The benefits extend beyond individual moves. Better coordination can shorten vessel turnaround times, minimize yard congestion and rehandles, and increase equipment utilization. By reducing waiting and avoidable work, terminals can unlock capacity hidden within their existing footprint and resources. By Harrison Nguyen

The Erik Mathiesen-led investment company has offered NOK6.30 per share in cash through wholly owned subsidiary HG Projectco 1, valuing Jacktel at an 8.6% premium to its November 18 closing share price. The bid has already secured commitments from six major Jacktel shareholders controlling around 73% of the company, including investment vehicles linked to chairman Harald Thorstein and Hunter board member Morten Astrup. Hunter needs acceptances representing more than 90% of Jacktel’s shares to complete the transaction. The offer was initially set to expire at 9 am Oslo time on November 20, with the option of extending the deadline to November 23. If successful, Hunter intends to buy out the remaining shareholders and delist Jacktel from Euronext Growth Oslo. The acquisition would be financed from available cash. Jacktel owns the four-legged, self-elevating accommodation rig Haven , which can house up to 444 offshore personnel and has been deployed on major North Sea oil and gas developments. The unit is currently working for Aker BP at the Valhall field, where its firm contract runs until February 2028, with options potentially extending employment through June that year. Jacktel reported 100% utilisation during the third quarter, generating $19m in revenue and $10.3m in EBITDA. Its firm contract backlog stood at $56m at the end of September, rising to $75m including options. The acquisition would mark another change of direction for Hunter, which has spent much of this year cashing in on historically strong VLCC rates through two back-to-back charter arrangements. The company chartered in the tankers at fixed rates averaging $51,750 per day before placing them on index-linked contracts, capturing substantial margins as tanker rates surged. Hunter’s latest results show a net time charter result of $114.2m in the third quarter, with its spot-linked charter rates averaging $673,342 per day against fixed charter-in costs of $51,750, leaving a margin of $621,592 per day. The company recorded a net profit of $111.4m for the quarter and reported $137.1m in cash and working capital at the end of September. The bumper earnings have continued into the fourth quarter, with Hunter fixing 53% of available vessel days at an average of approximately $1.35m per day. November rates have so far averaged around $1.25m per day. The VLCC arrangements are approaching expiry, leaving Hunter looking for a new source of longer-term earnings. SplashTech sought out experts throughout the week to provide readers plenty of advice on this issue, as well as issuing a podcast on this urgent matter . Caravel Group chief executive Angad Banga warned that the concentration of shipping’s digital infrastructure could expose thousands of vessels to simultaneous disruption. “The cyber risk I worry about most is concentration. Much of the global fleet relies on the same handful of chart systems, satellite networks and software platforms. If one is compromised, thousands of ships could be affected at once. In that sense, the industry’s uneven adoption of technology provides an accidental hedge: a fleet that does not all fail in the same way is a more resilient fleet,” Banga observed in a Caravel whitepaper published this week. The lessons extend well beyond conventional cybersecurity. Shipping companies need to understand their digital dependencies, particularly where multiple applications rely on the same underlying infrastructure. Backup systems must be genuinely independent, critical information accessible offline and procedures for continuing operations regularly tested. “We can’t eliminate the possibility of disruption entirely; however, by identifying vulnerabilities, avoiding reliance on a single system and preparing for different scenarios, maritime businesses can limit disruption when systems fail and maintain essential operations,” Jamie Jones, managing director of GTMaritime, wrote in an op-ed for SplashTech today . Another keenly read contribution this week came from Wolfgang Lehmacher who warned readers that from the Strait of Hormuz to the server halls of the Gulf, global trade is discovering a new vulnerability . articles.body: The Port of Koper handled 972,298 TEUs during the first nine months of 2026, representing a 2% increase compared with the same period last year. According to port operator Luka Koper, growth was supported by new business opportunities and more stable shipping services connecting the Far East with Northern Adriatic ports. Additional demand came from investments in automotive and battery manufacturing facilities across the port’s hinterland markets. Meanwhile, the Luka Koper Group reported net sales revenue of €308.8 million, up 9% year-on-year. Operating profit increased by 11% to €82.8 million, while net profit rose by 17% to €72.9 million. The results came despite ongoing uncertainty in international trade and changing cargo flows across European markets. Port investments reach €128.4 million Luka Koper invested €128.4 million during the January–September period, an increase of 57% compared with the same period in 2025. The investment programme includes the expansion of the northern section of the container quay and the reorganisation of storage blocks at the container terminal. Other ongoing projects include a multi-storey car park, a new berth at Pier II and a warehouse for steel coils. These developments form part of the port’s wider efforts to expand its handling capacity and improve operational efficiency. While container traffic increased, vehicle throughput declined by 6% to 646,209 units. The company attributed the decrease mainly to weaker exports by European manufacturers to markets in the Eastern Mediterranean and Far East. Luka Koper forecasts further container growth Looking ahead, Luka Koper expects container throughput to reach approximately 1.286 million TEUs by the end of 2026. The group also forecasts full-year net sales revenue of €410.1 million, representing an 8% increase compared with 2025. Investment spending is expected to reach €180.9 million for the full year. For 2027, the port operator is targeting a further 4% increase in container throughput to 1.338 million TEUs. However, the company noted that capacity constraints within the port and ongoing railway infrastructure upgrades could continue to affect operations. The latest results underline Koper’s role as a Northern Adriatic gateway for containerised trade between Asia and Central European markets.

articles.body: Asia Containers Dry Cargo Operations Regulatory Tankers Uncategorized India scraps compulsory retirement age for ships Adis Ajdin November 20, 2026 0 305 1 minute read Teekay Teekay India has scrapped compulsory retirement ages for ships flying its flag, reversing a policy designed to push older tonnage out of the country’s merchant fleet. The Directorate General of Maritime Administration (DGMA) issued a new order this week 18 allowing existing Indian-flagged vessels to continue trading regardless of age, provided they meet prescribed technical and safety standards. The government has also relaxed restrictions on bringing older vessels onto the Indian register. Tankers, bulk carriers and general cargo ships over 20 years old can now be considered for registration, subject to a technical review and approval process. For containerships, gas carriers and chemical tankers, the corresponding threshold is 25 years. Ships below those limits remain subject to graduated inspection and classification requirements depending on their age. The latest move overturns restrictions introduced in 2023 and revised in January this year, which had imposed firm age limits on ships entering and remaining in the Indian fleet. Shipowners had argued that age alone was a poor measure of a vessel’s condition and that continued operation should depend on inspections, maintenance and commercial acceptance. Under the new rules, a standing five-member technical committee will review requests involving ships above the normal entry thresholds. The maritime administration will retain the final say on whether individual vessels qualify. The revised standards also extend to foreign-flagged ships operating in India’s coastal trade under the Coastal Shipping Act 2025. They do not impose a general age restriction on every foreign ship making an international port call in India. The relaxation could help owners seeking to transfer older ships to the Indian flag, including containerline MSC, whose previously announced plan to register about a dozen vessels in India had reportedly encountered difficulties under the earlier age rules. articles.title: Who calls the shots when it comes to ship finance in Hong Kong?
articles.summary: Tax incentives, Chinese leasing capital and a deep banking network are keeping Hong Kong relevant to global shipping. But the industry’s biggest question is whether deals are genuinely made in the city, or merely booked there. A major containership financing this autumn illustrates both Hong Kong’s reach and its...
articles.body: Finance and Insurance Greater China Who calls the shots when it comes to ship finance in Hong Kong? Splash November 20, 2026 0 502 4 minutes read Victor Halder Victor Halder Tax incentives, Chinese leasing capital and a deep banking network are keeping Hong Kong relevant to global shipping. But the industry’s biggest question is whether deals are genuinely made in the city, or merely booked there. A major containership financing this autumn illustrates both Hong Kong’s reach and its limitations. Global Ship Lease’s new $1bn syndicated facility includes Bank of China (Hong Kong) and BOCOM Hong Kong among eight lenders supporting 15 newbuildings. But Bank of America is the bookrunner, and the money comes from a syndicate spanning three continents. A vessel can be ordered in China, owned through another jurisdiction, financed by multiple banks and leased to a charterer thousands of miles away. Where, then, does the financial centre sit? Hong Kong is determined that the answer should increasingly be Hong Kong. The government’s 2026 Policy Address introduced a Finance + Shipping agenda, promising closer integration of ship lending, marine insurance, common-law documentation and arbitration. The aim is to become more than a location for leasing vehicles. The backdrop is an expanding global financing market. Petrofin calculates that the world’s 40 largest shipping banks held $300.6bn in loans at the end of 2025, up 6% year-on-year, while leasing and alternative capital providers are taking an increasingly important role. Hong Kong is hardly starting from nothing. Hong Kong Trade Development Council figures show HK$105bn ($13.5bn) in shipping loans and advances booked locally at the end of June, equivalent to 1.4% of loans for use in Hong Kong. Some overseas-booked loans involving Hong Kong professionals are not captured in that total. Richard Hext, chairman of the Hong Kong Shipowners Association, rejects the idea that finance either originates in Hong Kong or is controlled entirely from Beijing and Shanghai. “Modern ship finance is often originated, structured, syndicated, insured and documented across several centres,” he says. Hong Kong’s opportunity is to assemble those functions around its banks, common-law contracts, capital markets and proximity to mainland Chinese shipping customers. The growth of ship leasing Ship leasing is where policy has delivered the most measurable growth. Since 2020, qualifying ship lessors have enjoyed a zero profits-tax rate, while eligible leasing managers receive an 8.25% rate. Government figures show the number of qualifying leasing enterprises rose from 11 in 2020/21 to 46 in 2022/23. But enterprise numbers do not measure loans originated or jobs created. The business has genuine scale. Hong Kong-listed CSSC Shipping, backed by China State Shipbuilding Corporation, had 130 vessels in its leasing portfolio, including 23 under construction, as of June. This year it raised HK$2.338bn in convertible bonds, while its growing fleet business illustrates the links between Chinese yards, capital markets and vessel leasing. Independent firms add another dimension. SeaKapital, established in 2023 by shipowner Sabrina Chao and former Credit Agricole Asia Shipfinance chief Kenneth Lam, aims to connect shipping assets with international investors from its Hong Kong base. However, local incorporation does not automatically mean local control. KC Maritime chairman Gautam Chellaram draws an important distinction between international banks and independent leasing businesses that make financing decisions in the city and major mainland leasing groups whose pricing, credit approvals and portfolio strategy are largely set across the border. “I believe Hong Kong is doing both, depending on which part of the market we consider,” he says. Chellaram sees little clear evidence that tax breaks alone have brought substantial relocations of head offices, investment mandates and senior decision-makers. “Tax is necessary but not sufficient,” Hext says. What matters is attracting people with real lending authority, not just low-tax structures. The mainland bridge Angad Banga, chief executive of The Caravel Group, argues that the question should not be reduced to a contest between Hong Kong and the mainland. “Shipping finance is increasingly collaborative rather than concentrated in a single city,” he says. Hong Kong connects global capital and legal expertise to China’s enormous trading and shipbuilding economy. Singapore nevertheless remains a formidable competitor. Its maritime authority identifies more than 20 major banks with ship-finance portfolios, alongside shipping trusts, investment banks and private equity providers. Beyond tax incentives, its concentration of charterers, commodity traders and commercial principals brings lenders physically closer to customers and decisions. New legislation Hong Kong’s concessions are being updated. Legislation introduced in June proposed improved tax treatment of ship acquisition costs for qualifying operating lessors, alongside an elective 15% tax-rate option aimed at reducing compliance complexity for multinational groups subject to international minimum-tax rules. The broader package also targeted physical commodity traders, whose presence could deepen the city’s commercial shipping network. Bjorn Hojgaard, chief executive of Anglo-Eastern, sees scope for expansion, particularly as fleet renewal and decarbonisation demand more capital. “Hong Kong has the banking, capital-markets and advisory depth to play a larger role in ship finance, leasing and green maritime investment than it does today,” he says. Hong Kong’s five-year plan identifies green newbuildings, retrofits and cross-border renminbi settlement as opportunities. But financing the transition means assessing future fuel availability, charter income, technology risk and residual ship values. Chellaram proposes a commercially underwritten first-loss guarantee and co-investment facility for cleaner ships and related infrastructure. Such a scheme would involve more direct risk-sharing than another tax break. Geopolitics Another test is geopolitical. Splash has reported Chinese lessors turning to Maltese flag structures to rebuild financing relationships with European owners as China-related commercial concerns mount. Hong Kong’s separate legal and financial system can facilitate cross-border transactions, but cannot entirely remove the political risks perceived by counterparties. Firoze Mirza, chairman of BSM Hong Kong, describes ship finance and leasing as part of an increasingly integrated mainland-Hong Kong financial system. “This is not a matter of ‘who leads’, but of how the whole system can more effectively serve the maritime economy,” he says. Hext argues the decisive measures should be local underwriting authority, credit decisions, trading desks, skilled jobs and headquarters, rather than company registrations alone. The territory remains a substantial ship finance centre, not merely a postal address. But the next stage of its revival depends on persuading more financiers not just to sign and book deals in Hong Kong, but to make the decisions there. articles.body: Americas Offshore US contractors win subsea package on Australian LNG megaproject Bojan Lepic November 20, 2026 0 449 1 minute read Inpex Inpex A consortium comprising US offshore contractors McDermott and Baker Hughes has secured a subsea engineering, procurement, construction and installation (EPCI) contract from Japan’s Inpex for the next development phase of the Ichthys LNG project offshore Western Australia. The award was made under the consortium’s existing subsea development framework agreement with Inpex and includes commissioning new subsea infrastructure that will tie into the project’s existing offshore production system. Baker Hughes will supply subsea trees, controls, wellheads, and associated services, while McDermott will provide engineering, fabrication and installation capabilities. The project will be managed from Perth, with additional engineering work carried out at McDermott’s facilities in Kuala Lumpur and Chennai. Fabrication will take place at the company’s Batam yard in Indonesia. The contract follows Inpex’s decision earlier this month to sanction Phase 2c Part 1 of the Ichthys development, which will involve drilling five additional production wells targeting the Brewster reservoir. The new wells will utilise existing offshore drilling centres and infrastructure to help sustain production and improve recovery from the field. Ichthys is located in the Browse Basin, approximately 220 km off Australia’s northwest coast, and has the capacity to produce up to 9.3m tonnes of LNG annually. The latest development follows the Phase 2a subsea expansion and Phase 2b booster compression project, both designed to support production from the offshore gas field. articles.title: Electrical Upgrades Logistics Facilities in Indianapolis Should Prioritize
articles.summary: Logistics facilities in Indianapolis should prioritize electrical upgrades that improve power capacity, reduce downtime, and support growing equipment demands. articles.body: Logistics facilities in Indianapolis should prioritize electrical upgrades that improve power capacity, reduce downtime, and support growing equipment demands. Modernizing electrical panels, installing energy-efficient lighting, upgrading power distribution systems, and adding backup power solutions can help warehouses maintain productivity during busy shipping periods. It’s the middle of a major shipping rush, and a conveyor suddenly stops working. Orders pile up as workers discover that the facility’s aging electrical system cannot handle the demand. Even a brief interruption can disrupt delivery schedules and leave customers waiting. For Indianapolis logistics operators, investing in the right electrical improvements now could prevent expensive operational headaches later. Modernizing Electrical Distribution Systems Warehouses depend on electrical panels and distribution systems that can handle demanding workloads. Older facilities may struggle to support additional machinery, especially when businesses introduce automated sorting equipment or expand operating hours. Facility managers should assess existing electrical capacity before installing new equipment. An electrical load assessment can reveal overloaded circuits, aging panels, and areas requiring additional capacity. Working with an Indianapolis commercial electrician from Facility Solutions Group can help businesses evaluate their electrical infrastructure and plan appropriate upgrades. Upgrading electrical infrastructure before expanding operations can also prevent expensive modifications later. Installing Energy-Efficient Warehouse Lighting Poor lighting can slow warehouse operations and make it harder for employees to identify potential hazards. Distribution centers with high ceilings also face significant maintenance challenges when outdated fixtures require frequent replacement. LED high-bay lighting provides an efficient alternative to traditional warehouse fixtures. These systems can improve visibility across storage aisles and reduce electricity consumption. Modern lighting controls offer additional opportunities to manage energy costs. Occupancy sensors can dim lights in unoccupied storage areas, and daylight-responsive controls can reduce unnecessary artificial lighting near windows. Match commercial lighting systems to specific tasks and use controls to avoid unnecessary consumption. Upgrading Forklift Charging Infrastructure Electric forklifts support daily operations in many Indianapolis distribution centers. However, expanding an electric fleet without upgrading charging infrastructure can place additional pressure on existing circuits. Warehouse managers should evaluate charging capacity before purchasing more battery-powered equipment. Dedicated electrical circuits and appropriately rated charging stations can help prevent overloads. Charging areas also require careful safety planning. Lead-acid battery charging areas need precautions addressing ventilation and potential exposure to hazardous substances. Facility managers should also protect charging equipment from forklift collisions and establish designated charging spaces. Planning for future fleet expansion can help businesses avoid repeated electrical renovations. Improving Loading Dock Electrical Systems Loading docks handle constant activity, so reliable electrical connections are especially important. Powered dock levelers, overhead doors, and vehicle restraints can experience operational problems when electrical components deteriorate. Facilities should inspect wiring and control panels around loading areas for signs of damage. Frequent equipment cycling and moisture exposure can contribute to electrical problems. Upgrading dock controls can improve equipment reliability and reduce interruptions during busy shipping periods. Exterior lighting improvements can also help employees navigate loading areas during overnight operations. Installing Reliable Backup Power Power outages can interrupt warehouse operations even when they last only a short time. Automated equipment may need to restart, and temperature-sensitive inventory may face additional risks. Backup generators can support essential systems during extended electrical interruptions. However, facility managers should identify critical electrical loads before selecting equipment. Uninterruptible power supplies offer another option for equipment that cannot tolerate even brief power interruptions. These systems can protect network hardware and allow certain automated controls to shut down safely. Facilities should test backup systems regularly and confirm that equipment can support the intended electrical loads. Strengthening Electrical Safety and Maintenance Preventive maintenance helps logistics facilities identify electrical problems before they interrupt operations. Aging connections and damaged insulation may remain unnoticed until equipment begins malfunctioning. Regular inspections can identify deteriorating components and potential overheating. Qualified electrical professionals can also evaluate protective devices and recommend necessary repairs. Maintenance plans should account for heavy equipment usage and the facility’s operating schedule. Coordinating inspections during planned downtime can minimize interruptions to warehouse activities. Facility managers should also review applicable electrical requirements before undertaking renovations. Introducing Smart Energy Monitoring High electricity bills don’t always show where a warehouse is wasting energy. Monitoring systems can provide more detailed information about equipment consumption and peak demand. Facility managers can use electrical monitoring technology to identify unusual consumption patterns and evaluate equipment performance. Reviewing this information can help determine which upgrades deserve immediate attention. For example, managers can adjust charging schedules to reduce simultaneous demand from multiple forklifts. Monitoring can also reveal equipment operating unnecessarily outside scheduled production hours. Preparing Indianapolis Logistics Facilities for Growth Electrical upgrades can help Indianapolis logistics facilities maintain dependable operations and control long-term expenses. Prioritizing improvements based on equipment demands and existing infrastructure helps businesses invest where upgrades will make the greatest difference. articles.title: Greece Has The Most To Lose From Delays In Shipping’s Green Transition, New Analysis Finds
articles.summary: Greek shipowners hold around USD 78bn of assets exposed to the global energy transition, twice the exposure of Japan, the next most exposed ship owning nation. The risk relates to declining demand for fossil fuel cargoes which could reduce the need for vessels such as LNG carriers. It is separate but related to the...
articles.body: Greece Has The Most To Lose From Delays In Shipping’s Green Transition, New Analysis Finds in International Shipping News 20/11/2026 Greek shipowners hold around USD 78bn of assets exposed to the global energy transition, twice the exposure of Japan, the next most exposed ship owning nation. The risk relates to declining demand for fossil fuel cargoes which could reduce the need for vessels such as LNG carriers. It is separate but related to the risks faced by all shipowners as they manage the energy transition that will also take place within international shipping, whether driven by IMO regulation adopted this December, or postponed global regulation accompanied by a patchwork of regional regulation. The new report finds that the IMO Net-Zero Framework (NZF) is the most credible route to the single global rulebook that the shipping industry, including the Union of Greek Shipowners (UGS) has called for. A weaker, technical-only outcome at the IMO would leave the EU Emissions Trading System (ETS) alongside the IMO fuel standard, as well as incentivising additions to other unilateral carbon pricing such as those already started in Africa – which is the regional patchwork UGS warns against. Greece owns about a fifth of the world fleet, roughly 5,800 ships and 460 million deadweight tonnes (dwt). Greek shipowners collectively have particularly leading market shares in ownership of the oil tankers, LNG carriers and bulk carriers that move fossil fuels, making them more exposed to transition risks than any other nation. Owners cannot change demand for fossil fuel cargoes, but they can influence how shipping is regulated. The report finds that the NZF would give them a predictable timetable, more compliance options and a managed exit from LNG exposure, reducing the risk of stranded assets. Dr Tristan Smith, Professor of Energy and Transport at UCL Energy Insitute and co-director of the Shipping and Oceans Research Group said “Greek owners already face one transition they cannot control, which is related to changes in the demand for the cargoes their ships carry. Supporting the NZF, the only adoptable architecture on the table at MEPC 85, is a chance to make the second one, in how shipping’s own energy transition is regulated, predictable, lower burden, less complicated and more supportive of a mix of decarbonisation strategies and pathways.” The report, Real economy consequences for Greece from success or failure of the Net-Zero Framework, is published ahead of ISWG-GHG 23 (23 to 27 November) and MEPC 85, which opens on 30 November. At MEPC 84, NZF-like options drew more than twice the support of technical-only alternatives. Earlier this week, UGS President Melina Travlos urged IMO member states to deliver a regulation that is “pragmatic, proportionate and implementable”, and questioned whether the EU is putting its regional measures, and the revenues they generate, ahead of a global deal. The report draws a similar concern about the risk of regulatory fragmentation, particularly how this could disadvantage smaller shipping companies with less capacity and flexibility to manage the administrative burden and timing of shipping’s energy transition. The report finds there is no alternative architecture to NZF that has anywhere close to the levels of support for adoption and efforts that do not support NZF are only increasing risks of stalemate and fragmentation. The European Commission’s commitment to avoid double payment depends on a global carbon price being adopted, so without one, the EU ETS would stay in force on top of the IMO standard. Demetres Karavellas, CEO of WWF Greece said “As climate impacts intensify, shipping must play its part in the transition to net-zero. The IMO Net-Zero Framework is the only credible global pathway to decarbonise the sector while providing the certainty businesses need to invest. This report shows that Greece, as the world’s leading shipping nation, has more to lose from delay than almost anyone else. Opposing the NZF will not stop the transition. It will only increase uncertainty and expose Greek shipping to greater risk. Greece has an opportunity to help shape a global framework rather than face a more fragmented and disruptive transition later.” The report concludes that failure to adopt the NZF, or a delay of more than a year, would weaken the IMO as global regulator, accelerate regional regulation and force a steeper decarbonisation pathway later. The report urges shipowners to engage constructively in developing the NZF and its guidelines, as the only viable, truly global framework. articles.summary: While the larger Capesize ship class continues to act as a benchmark for the broader dry bulk market, smaller sizes have shown significant diversion over the past few days. articles.body: Dry Bulk Market: Kamsarmax Rebounds, Soybeans Set Records in Hellenic Shipping News 20/11/2026 W hile the larger Capesize ship class continues to act as a benchmark for the broader dry bulk market, smaller sizes have shown significant diversion over the past few days. In its latest weekly report, shipbroker Xclusiv commented that “the dry bulk market continues to demonstrate contrasting dynamics across the Kamsarmax and Ultramax segments, although the considerable earnings differential observed in late October has narrowed during the first half of November. According to Baltic Exchange data, average Kamsarmax earnings (P5TC) increased by 5.7% week-on-week, reaching USD 19,063/day on 13 November, compared with USD 16,999/day at the end of October. Meanwhile, Ultramax earnings (S11TC) stood at USD 23,203/day, recording a more modest weekly increase of 1.1%. Consequently, the earnings differential between the two segments has narrowed from USD 6,570/day on 30 October to approximately USD 4,140/day, reflecting an improvement in Kamsarmax market conditions”. Source: Xclusiv shipbroker According to Xclusiv, “despite this recent recovery, Kamsarmax earnings remain 11.2% below their end-September levels, highlighting the persistent pressure facing the segment. The divergence between the two vessel classes continues to reflect differences in cargo exposure, regional tonnage availability and trading flexibility. Kamsarmax vessels remain particularly dependent on coal and grain movements, while Ultramaxes benefit from a more diversified cargo base, including minor bulks, fertilizers, steel products and agricultural commodities. Their onboard cranes also provide greater flexibility in serving smaller ports and terminals with limited infrastructure”. “Against this backdrop, developments in the Brazilian soybean trade offer an encouraging perspective for dry bulk demand. According to market data, Brazil exported a record 108.4 million tonnes of soybeans during January–October 2026, representing a 7.9% increase year-on-year. Remarkably, shipments during these ten months have already exceeded the entire 2025 volume by approximately 600,000 tonnes. Second-quarter exports reached 44.9 million tonnes, up 10.3% year-on-year, while third-quarter volumes increased by 8.1% to 29.7 million tonnes”, the shipbroker said. Meanwhile, “these developments are particularly relevant for the Panamax/Kamsarmax and Supramax/Ultramax segments, which play an important role in agricultural commodity transportation. With China remaining the principal destination for Brazilian soybeans, continued growth in exports could generate additional tonne-mile demand, especially as long-haul Brazil–Asia shipments absorb vessel capacity for extended periods. Nevertheless, the seasonal distribution of Brazilian exports remains an important consideration. October shipments declined by almost 14% compared with September, reflecting the gradual winding down of the previous harvest season. Therefore, although annual export volumes have reached record levels, their immediate contribution to freight market strength may remain uneven, depending on shipment timing and available tonnage”, Xclusiv noted. Source: Xclusiv shipbroker The shipbroker added that “looking further ahead, the outlook remains constructive. The USDA projects Brazil’s 2026/27 soybean production at 186 million tonnes, with exports expected to reach 118 million tonnes. If realised, these volumes could provide further support to dry bulk employment during the upcoming export season, particularly across long-haul routes towards Asia. In the near term, winter coal demand and North American grain shipments could also contribute to improving Kamsarmax employment. However, stronger electricity consumption does not necessarily translate into higher seaborne coal imports, particularly when inventories remain sufficient or domestic production covers additional requirements”. Xclusiv concluded that “overall, while the recent narrowing of the Kamsarmax–Ultramax earnings gap suggests some rebalancing between the segments, sustained recovery will depend on stronger cargo volumes absorbing available vessel supply. Record Brazilian soybean exports provide a positive underlying demand signal, but regional tonnage distribution, seasonal trade patterns and actual tonne-mile growth will remain decisive in determining freight market direction”. articles.title: Get your data in order and set a course for greener shipping
articles.summary: There is cause for optimism in the shipping sector, and we are seeing more and more initiatives aimed at making shipping greener. Shipowners are now far more willing to reduce emissions from ships than they were just a few years ago. That said, we must also acknowledge that the shipping industry has a data problem, ...
articles.body: Get your data in order and set a course for greener shipping in International Shipping News 20/11/2026 T here is cause for optimism in the shipping sector, and we are seeing more and more initiatives aimed at making shipping greener. Shipowners are now far more willing to reduce emissions from ships than they were just a few years ago. That said, we must also acknowledge that the shipping industry has a data problem, which means shipowners are not getting the insights needed to accelerate the green transition. In the coming weeks alone, there are two events worth keeping an eye on. From 23 to 27 November, the IMO’s working group known as ISWG-GHG 23 will continue its discussions on a global Net-Zero Framework – that is, proposals for common, global climate rules designed to steer the shipping industry towards net-zero emissions by 2050. A few days later, from 30 November to 3 December, the IMO’s Marine Environment Protection Committee (MEPC) will convene for MEPC 85, with emissions, energy efficiency and environmental protection, amongst other topics, on the agenda. There remains disagreement over the way forward, but the work being done within the IMO, amongst others, demonstrates a willingness to find common solutions. I sense the same willingness when I speak to shipping companies and other industry stakeholders. Compared with just three years ago, there is far greater interest in concrete climate action. René Bredmose Christensen, Green Instruments However, although progress is being made, the shipping industry still has a data problem. We still know too little about the emissions of individual ships and how they can reduce their fuel consumption. Far too many people still rely on calculations that are, at best, uncertain and, at worst, misleading. Shipowners cannot navigate between new requirements and regulations blindfolded. They need valid data to set the right course. Calculations and standard values do not reveal how engines perform during operation or how high emissions really are. In the coming years, shipping companies will have to deal with the use of multiple fuels, technologies and types of emissions. How do they assess emissions from different fuels whilst at sea? How do they demonstrate that an investment reduces emissions? And how do they determine the engine settings that deliver the lowest fuel consumption? Here, real-time measurements are a crucial tool – for documentation, compliance with requirements and day-to-day decision-making. The new five-year partnership between the Global Centre for Maritime Decarbonisation (GCMD) and Equinor is a strong example of how the green transition requires joint efforts and practical trials. They will collaborate on areas including alternative fuels, energy efficiency and CO₂ management. Their emphasis on documentation and verification is entirely appropriate. After all, shipowners and organisations can only derive the full benefit from such initiatives if they have access to valid data. I therefore hope that they will involve experts in emissions measurement to a greater extent at an early stage of the process. This increases the likelihood that we can actually learn from each other’s experiences. At the same time, shipowners can take advantage of some straightforward opportunities. Linking real-time measurements to the engines’ operational data would enable shipping companies to identify which operating conditions increase fuel consumption and emissions. However, without the necessary equipment on board, these opportunities are easily overlooked. With valid data, shipping companies can act immediately to reduce costs and cut emissions. I hope that the IMO meetings will bring the shipping industry closer to achieving common climate regulations. However, these regulations cannot stand alone. The green course must be set collectively and guided by what we can measure and document. Source: By Rene B. Christensen, CEO, Green Instruments Tops 2026-11-20 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

That said, we must also acknowledge that the shipping industry has a data problem, which means shipowners are not getting the insights needed to accelerate the green transition.
