articles.title: Smart Sea urges shipowners to tackle ageing infrastructure before investing in new digital solutions
articles.summary: Shipowners risk undermining their digitalisation efforts by investing in new technology while continuing to operate outdated and potentially vulnerable IT systems, according to maritime technology consultancy SmartSea. Recent fleet assessments by the company have identified vessels still running unsupported operating...
articles.body: Smart Sea urges shipowners to tackle ageing infrastructure before investing in new digital solutions in International Shipping News 20/11/2026 Shipowners risk undermining their digitalisation efforts by investing in new technology while continuing to operate outdated and potentially vulnerable IT systems, according to maritime technology consultancy SmartSea. Recent fleet assessments by the company have identified vessels still running unsupported operating systems, including Windows 7, raising concerns over cybersecurity, system reliability and the ability to integrate modern digital applications. Kris Vedat, CEO of Smart Sea, warns that too many operators are prioritising new software and connectivity over the infrastructure needed to support them. “We’re still finding vessels running operating systems that have been unsupported for years,” said Mr Vedat. “That’s a cybersecurity risk and a major obstacle to digitalisation. There’s little point investing in sophisticated technology if the underlying systems aren’t fit for purpose.” Mr Vedat believes the industry needs to move away from short-term technology fixes towards a more co-ordinated approach that includes infrastructure assessments, standardised processes and phased implementation. “Crew training is essential, but it’s only part of the solution. Digital transformation isn’t about buying more software. It’s about making sure the systems, processes and people are ready to make it work,” he explained. The SmartSea CEO also cautions against focusing too heavily on short-term savings. Cheaper satellite connectivity, for example, can quickly become a false economy if poor integration, unreliable data flows or security weaknesses create additional operational costs. Kris Vedat, CEO, SmartSea Mr Vedat said: “Saving money upfront means very little if it creates bigger problems down the line. Technology investments should be judged on the operational value they deliver, not simply the immediate cost savings.” The lack of consistent technical standards across shipping adds to the challenge, particularly for third-party ship managers inheriting vessels with ageing IT and operational technology. Smart Sea believes clearer minimum standards would help improve cybersecurity and support more effective fleet-wide digitalisation. Mr Vedat believes addressing these technical and commercial barriers is essential if shipping is to realise the full potential of digitalisation, automation and decarbonisation technologies. He added: “Shipping doesn’t have a shortage of technology. The challenge is making it work effectively. Operators need to stop chasing quick fixes and focus on getting the foundations right. Otherwise, they risk spending more on technology without seeing the benefits.” Source: Smart Sea 2026-11-20 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.body: Drewry: Asia-Europe capacity returns via Suez – but security concerns remain in International Shipping News 20/11/2026 Drewry’s Red Sea Diversion Tracker delivers timely intelligence to shippers, carriers, ports and other stakeholders on the evolving structure of carrier networks. This tracker page is updated fortnightly (every other Tuesday). During the week ended 15 Nov, a total of 57 containerships transited the Suez Canal (in either direction), up 73% when compared with the number in the same week of 2025, with 60% of Asia-Europe capacity now using the Suez route again. There have now been 7 weeks with more than 50 Suez transits a week, indicating a continued momentum in the return of containerships from the Cape of Good Hope route to the Suez route. The average number of transits via Suez was 54 in the latest 3 weeks, about the same as in the previous three weeks. The number of transits around the Cape of Good Hope continued to decline during the week ended 15 Nov, with only 126 transits, the lowest weekly total since January 2026. 17 NOV: SECURITY WATCH Material deterioration in Bab al-Mandeb security situation: While encouraging to see the steady return of transits via Red Sea and Suez, in recent days there has been a material deterioration in the security situation in the vicinity of Bab al-Mandab with government forces withdrawing from their positions overlooking the Strait. This creates an uncomfortable strategic picture for commercial shipping – returning to the Red Sea just as the Houthis re-establish their position around this important maritime chokepoint. Source: Drewry Container Capacity Insight Improving Red Sea traffic figures should therefore be treated with caution and not extrapolated to set expectations for December and January. In a statement to Iran’s state broadcaster, the paramilitary group said the ships were carrying over 4 million barrels of crude and attempting to traverse the southern section of Hormuz under the protection of the U.S. military. The Associated Press said the Iranian claims could not be immediately verified and U.S. Central Command, which oversees U.S. forces in the Middle East, did not comment. Tehran has frequently warned ships against transiting Hormuz, a vital waterway for a fifth of the world’s oil and liquefied natural gas before the start of the U.S.-Israel assault on Iran in late February. Iran has moved to close down the strait, although shipments have begun to improve in recent months, fueling some predictions that global oil supply could soon outstrip demand. Benchmark Brent crude prices have fallen by more than fifth so far this month. However, in a potential sign of the impact of the Iranian attacks, crude shipments through the strait appear to have fallen since the start of November. Data firm Kpler said the number of shipments going through Hormuz have declined to 8.5 million barrels per day, or around half of the prewar levels reached at the beginning of the month. Still, Kpler flagged that shipments could recover over the rest of November. According to media reports, tanker crews have had to employ a ship-to-ship transit procedure to take oil barrels out of the Persian Gulf, a risky process that has sparked a surge in vessel chartering rates. Meanwhile, there have been few indications that the standoff in Hormuz is softening. U.S. President Donald Trump is weighing another round of extensive military strikes on Iran, considering fresh intelligence about Tehran’s military capabilities and mounting pressure from Israel to launch an aggressive campaign, The New York Times reported on Wednesday, citing U.S. and Israeli officials briefed on the discussions. Trump has not made a final decision, but is assessing Israeli warnings that Iran is rebuilding its missile and drone arsenals and advancing its chemical and biological weapons programs, the report said. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is pushing Washington to join Israel in a four- to seven-day campaign of airstrikes, seeking to capitalize on the U.S. military presence in the region, according to the report. articles.title: Court Ruling Threatens License for $2.1 Billion Texas Offshore Oil Export Project
articles.summary: A court ruling has jeopardized a license for Sentinel Midstream’s $2.1 billion deepwater crude oil export project off the Texas coast, an environmental group that petitioned the court said this week.
articles.body: Advertise Forum Jobs Subscribe Grab a Seat at the Captain’s Table Essential news coupled with the finest maritime content sourced from across the globe. Join the leading maritime news network Stock Photo: tcly / Shutterstock By Arathy Somasekhar HOUSTON, Nov 19 (Reuters) – A court ruling has jeopardized a license for Sentinel Midstream’s $2.1 billion deepwater crude oil export project off the Texas coast, an environmental group that petitioned the court said this week. The ruling, which took effect on October 30, poses a setback and likely delays for the oil transportation and storage company, which has already started work on the project. It could also impact other pending deepwater port applications. In August, a US appeals court voided a federal record of decision for Sentinel Midstream’s Texas GulfLink project, citing overlap with another deepwater project. An official at Sentinel Midstream said work would continue on the project, characterizing it as “business as usual.” But a source with knowledge of the situation said the company could not continue with the offshore project on the current license. Last year, the US Maritime Administration (MARAD), in its record of decision (ROD), approved Texas GulfLink with conditions and the company received its license in January 2026 . President Donald Trump has pushed for faster project approvals to bolster the US energy industry. Sentinel made a final investment decision in May and began construction. MARAD’s record of decision approving Texas GulfLink’s application violated the Deepwater Port Act’s requirement that only one deepwater port be approved per application area, the 5th US Circuit Court of Appeals said. Texas GulfLink’s application area, when properly designated, would have intersected with Enterprise Products Partners’ Sea Port Oil Terminal (SPOT) deepwater project. Congress has struck a careful balance between promoting and regulating the construction and operation of deepwater ports, the court said, holding that the Deepwater Port Act requires an application area to encompass the entirety of a proposed deepwater port site, including any proposed pipeline. “The Court’s decision is clear: it vacated the record of decision that was the foundation of GulfLink’s license. Now, MARAD has to revoke or suspend that license,” Michael Brown, a counsel for the petitioners, said on Wednesday. Construction of the project cannot continue without a federal deepwater port license, said environmental group Better Brazoria Clean Air and Water in a press release this week. MARAD said it was disappointed with the outcome and continues to pursue all avenues to achieve the President’s vision of American energy dominance. “Sentinel is working with MARAD to discuss its options for moving forward. The company cannot continue with the current license,” a source familiar with the matter said. In comments to Reuters this week, Sentinel said its license has not been suspended or terminated. Texas GulfLink, to be situated about 30 miles off Freeport, Texas, remains on track for a fourth-quarter 2028 operational date, Bruce Heine, a senior vice president at Sentinel, said this week, adding that given the narrow nature and scope of the issue, there are multiple paths to address the statutory concern without disrupting ongoing construction activities or overall project schedule. “It remains business as usual for Texas GulfLink, with site development and improvement activities currently underway at our Jones Creek onshore terminal facility as we prepare to commence tank construction,” Heine said, adding that major long-lead equipment and pipe have been purchased, and key construction contracts executed. However, the company in its motion last month to stay the court mandate said that the Texas GulfLink’s license expressly incorporates the ROD as a compliance standard, adding that voiding the ROD in turn exposed the license to suspension or revocation by MARAD, and prevents construction of offshore components. “At a minimum, the cloud on Texas GulfLink’s regulatory posture will harm Texas GulfLink in the marketplace,” the company said then, adding that “given the uncertainty of its ROD and license, Texas GulfLink will not commence construction of the deepwater port under the current posture, even if the mandate is stayed.” Texas GulfLink plans to petition the Supreme Court, the company said in its motion. It added that there are two other pending deepwater ports under review with application areas similar to Texas GulfLink’s that will likely require redesignation as a result of the panel’s decision, potentially resulting in consequential impacts to those projects as well. If Sentinel is required to resubmit its application, it would have to await a new ROD and license. While it took nearly seven years for Sentinel to secure approvals last time, MARAD has sped up its approval process under US President Donald Trump. It recently issued a deepwater project application license in just 410 days, nearly 3.7 years faster than ?the historical average. The Texas GulfLink project aims to fully load a supertanker with about 2 million barrels of oil per day. The administration in recent weeks also approved deepwater port license applications for Energy Transfer’s ET.N Blue Marlin Offshore Port, an oil export project off the Louisiana coast, and for ST LNG, which aims to ship liquefied natural gas off ?the Texas coast. articles.summary: American Roll-On Roll-Off Carrier Group Inc. (ARC Group) has welcomed ARC United to its U.S.-flagged fleet, expanding the company’s ability to transport vehicles, heavy equipment and military cargo in support of American commerce and national…
articles.body: ARC United Large Car, Truck Carrier Joins US Fleet for Military Support Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 19, 2026 © ARC Group American Roll-On Roll-Off Carrier Group Inc. (ARC Group) has welcomed ARC United to its U.S.-flagged fleet, expanding the company’s ability to transport vehicles, heavy equipment and military cargo in support of American commerce and national defense. ARC United is a 757-foot Large Car and Truck Carrier (LCTC) designed to transport vehicles, heavy equipment, breakbulk and project cargo. Through the Maritime Security Program, it will serve commercial and government customers in international trade while remaining available to support U.S. military requirements. ARC United is the ninth vessel in ARC's fleet capable of carrying V-22 Osprey and CH-47 Chinook aircraft. These large military aircraft require deck clearance and cargo access that commercial vessels are not typically built to provide, making ARC’s fleet particularly valuable for overseas deployments and U.S. military exercises with partners. ARC United has 13 cargo decks, including five with hoistable sections that accommodate cargo of varying heights with the ability to ship nearly 8,000 car-equivalent units. REUTERS/Gustavo Graf The Trump administration on Thursday completed the first-ever U.S. offshore critical minerals lease auction, drawing $6 million in high bids for more than 31.5 million acres of seabed off American Samoa despite mounting environmental opposition and a federal court ruling against a key part of the government’s environmental review. The Department of the Interior announced that its Marine Minerals Administration (MMA) completed the sale of two lease areas in federal waters, marking a major step in President Donald Trump’s push to develop domestic sources of critical minerals and reduce dependence on foreign supply chains. The two areas lie approximately 150 to 240 miles east of Pago Pago, in waters ranging from 4,630 to 20,100 feet deep. The $6 million in combined high bids matched the minimum asking price of $3 million for each area. Interior did not identify the winning bidders in its initial announcement. “This is the first time the United States has held an offshore critical minerals lease sale in the Pacific and a historic step for America’s energy and mineral security,” Interior Secretary Doug Burgum said. The leases are intended to support exploration for minerals contained in polymetallic nodules and ferromanganese crusts, which can contain metals used in batteries, electronics, defense equipment and other industrial applications. The sale comes just three days after a federal judge in Hawaii ruled that the National Marine Fisheries Service violated the Endangered Species Act in its review of the proposed lease sale. Despite that ruling, Interior proceeded with Thursday’s auction. Environmental group Oceana condemned the sale, warning that the move could open vast stretches of U.S. waters to commercial seabed mining. “The Trump administration has clearly put corporate interests above the health and well-being of our oceans,” said Julia Singer, Oceana’s defense campaign manager. “Mining in U.S. waters may begin off American Samoa, but make no mistake, it won’t stop there.” The lease areas are near the Rose Atoll Marine National Monument, a protected marine area that supports sea turtles, whales and other vulnerable species. Oceana said more than 76,000 public comments were submitted during an earlier stage of the leasing process, with the overwhelming majority opposing deep-sea mining. American Samoa Governor Pulaali’i Nikolao Pula has also expressed opposition to commercial mineral extraction in the territory’s waters. The debate centers in part on the potential damage from mining the deep seabed, including disturbance of poorly understood habitats, sediment plumes and impacts on marine ecosystems. The administration argues that access to offshore critical minerals could strengthen U.S. manufacturing and national security while reducing reliance on foreign suppliers. Thursday’s auction does not authorize mining to begin. According to Interior, the leases would provide limited rights to conduct preliminary activities and an exclusive opportunity to submit plans for further exploration, testing and commercial extraction. Those activities would require additional environmental reviews and regulatory approvals. The leases carry a 20-year primary term, with royalties beginning at 2% of production value for the first five years of commercial production before increasing to 5%. The auction also comes as the administration pursues additional offshore mineral leasing proposals near the Northern Mariana Islands and in federal waters off Alaska and Virginia. For now, the American Samoa sale represents a historic step toward a domestic deep-sea mining industry, but one that faces significant hurdles before any commercial minerals are recovered. articles.title: Sea-Intelligence: NAWC Import Growth at 17.6% in September
articles.summary: In 2026‑Q3, North America West Coast (NAWC) ports experienced steady overall volume growth, driven almost entirely by a 17.6% Y/Y surge in laden imports in September. Following a sluggish start to the quarter, where laden imports contracted by ‑3.9% Y/Y in July and stabilized in August, September volumes surged to...
articles.body: In 2026‑Q3, North America West Coast (NAWC) ports experienced steady overall volume growth, driven almost entirely by a 17.6% Y/Y surge in laden imports in September. Following a sluggish start to the quarter, where laden imports contracted by ‑3.9% Y/Y in July and stabilized in August, September volumes surged to 1.45 million TEU. This double‑digit percentage growth in September is partially exaggerated by an unusually weak 2025‑Q3 baseline, when laden import growth dropped by ‑12.5 percentage points between July and September 2025. Still, 2026 marks the highest September laden import volume on record for the West Coast, eclipsing the previous high set in 2024. Overall, for 2026-Q3, NAWC ports recorded a 2.6% Y/Y increase in total container volume throughput, bringing the aggregate volume to 8.32 million TEU for the quarter. This growth was heavily weighted towards inbound cargo, with laden imports growing by 3.9% to reach 4.12 million TEU. In contrast, outbound cargo experienced more muted growth, as laden exports increased by just 1.8% to 1.21 million TEU, and empty container exports saw a smaller increase of 1.1% Y/Y to 2.67 million TEU. The operational impact of this highly compressed peak season has been substantial. Rather than managing a smoothed‑out influx of seasonal cargo, terminals were forced to handle an 11.3% M/M jump in laden imports from August to September, which is the highest M/M September increase across the 2012 to 2026 period. This level of sudden volatility creates acute stress on port infrastructure, chassis availability, and rail networks. As shippers navigated this, they overwhelmingly prioritized the ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach, which captured 73% of the West Coast’s total laden imports in 2026‑Q3.

articles.title: Middle East Conflict Could Cut Global Oil Demand by 4%
articles.summary: The Middle East conflict has caused the biggest disruption ever to global oil and gas trade and could cut world oil demand by more than 4% by 2035 if governments accelerate electrification, efficiency and fuel-switching measures in response…
articles.body: Middle East Conflict Could Cut Global Oil Demand by 4% Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 19, 2026 © Adobe Stock/Yellow Boat The Middle East conflict has caused the biggest disruption ever to global oil and gas trade and could cut world oil demand by more than 4% by 2035 if governments accelerate electrification, efficiency and fuel-switching measures in response, the International Energy Agency (IEA) said on Thursday. Energy markets have been rattled this year by the conflict, which has curbed shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, a route that typically carries about a fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas supplies and is a key artery for Gulf exports. "In my view, the energy world will never be the same again as it was before the Iran war," IEA Executive Director Fatih Birol said in an interview alongside the release of the agency's World Energy Outlook 2026. The conflict has resulted in cumulative losses of 2.8 billion barrels of oil and 60 billion cubic metres (bcm) of gas supplies from the Gulf, the Paris-based agency said. The annual outlook includes a range of scenarios based on existing and proposed energy policies. This year it also examines how governments and markets could respond to prolonged disruption in Hormuz. Under a new Additional Response Case (ARC), the IEA said energy security concerns could speed up electrification, energy-efficiency measures and efforts to reduce dependence on imported fossil fuels. In that case, global oil demand in 2035 is 4.4 million barrels per day lower than under the agency's Stated Policies Scenario (STEPS), which reflects governments' current policy intentions. Electric vehicles alone would displace more than 11 million bpd of oil demand. Global oil demand falls to 97 million bpd in 2035 and 85 million bpd by 2050 under ARC, compared with just over 101 million bpd in 2035 under STEPS. Gas demand under ARC is more than 300 bcm lower than under STEPS. ELECTRIFICATION GROWING The report said electrification is now cost-competitive across large parts of transport, heating and industry, although inadequate grids, charging networks and power supplies could slow its rollout. "Many countries are seeing electrification as a policy option for energy security. Instead of importing energy, they decided to build energy at home," Birol said. Electricity's share of final energy consumption is projected to approach 30% globally under STEPS, up from about 23% today, as transport, heating and parts of industry switch away from fossil fuels. Alongside data centres, rising demand for cooling is emerging as one of the strongest drivers of electricity consumption. For the first time, demand for cooling in buildings has exceeded demand for heating, the IEA said, as higher temperatures and rising incomes drive rapid growth in air-conditioner use. articles.summary: Iran’s attacks on oil tankers crossing the crucial Strait of Hormuz are getting more intense, just as prices have tumbled due to a flood of supply from the Middle East.
articles.body: Advertise Forum Jobs Subscribe Grab a Seat at the Captain’s Table Essential news coupled with the finest maritime content sourced from across the globe. Join the leading maritime news network A massive fire engulfs what has been identified as the LPG tanker TARA GAS in the Strait of Hormuz. Reuters independently verified footage of the burning vessel, although the exact filming date could not be established. (Screenshot from video) (Bloomberg) — Iran’s attacks on oil tankers crossing the crucial Strait of Hormuz are getting more intense, just as prices have tumbled due to a flood of supply from the Middle East. After a period of low-grade clashes, attacks increased in October and continued at the higher tempo this month, according to data compiled by Bloomberg. In a sign of the mounting severity, at least two seafarers are missing after attacks this week. Traders and shipowners also circulated videos of a vessel engulfed in flames this week, though Bloomberg couldn’t immediately verify the footage. The flareups are happening as Brent crude futures slid about a fifth this month as Middle East exports approached pre-war levels, with the International Energy Agency last week saying that supply is outpacing demand for the first time since the war began. However, flows appear to have pulled back recently, though it’s not clear whether that’s due to intensifying attacks, with shipments often volatile from week to week and month to month. Critically, it’s also hard to quickly gauge how badly vessels are being hit as producers tend to remain tight-lipped due to security concerns. A key question is whether the attacks will be enough to meaningfully impact oil supply. “It seems like the new normal: Something like a war, but not exactly a war, with attacks on ships virtually every day,” said Georgios Sakellariou, an analyst at shipping-analytics platform Signal Ocean. “Oil is going out, but being certain about the volumes is complicated by the attacks and the secrecy.” Another issue is that while oil is flowing through Hormuz, more and more vessels will be needed as some are lost to attacks, he said. There are signs that attacks are becoming more serious. Several maritime security officials have said that Iran has attempted to hit the same ship on multiple occasions to deter salvors, and that there have also been sightings of limpet mines attached to vessels. One Gulf oil official said the situation in and around Hormuz had deteriorated since the US midterms. Gulf producers rely on energy exports to fund their economies. One senior Saudi shipping official said at a conference last week that the kingdom has no choice but to continue shipping oil through Hormuz, despite the attacks. Traders, analysts and shipping officials generally collate data from UK Maritime Trade Operations and the International Maritime Organization to assess the severity of attacks. But Gulf producers rarely release public information about attacks to help protect the security of vessels. So far this month, UKMTO has reported roughly one attack a day, with about 14 incidents occurring in Hormuz. Last month, it said it was struggling to accurately report the number of attacks as many companies weren’t reporting incidents to authorities. That’s fueling uncertainty about exactly how many attacks there are, as well as rampant rumors and speculation on vessels within commodity trading circles. While there’s also uncertainty about flows through Hormuz, there are signs that they have fallen from elevated levels this month, according to data from intelligence firms Kpler and Vortexa. The seven-day moving average of oil transits through Hormuz and net ship-to-ship transfers in the Gulf of Oman eased to about 10 million barrels a day by Nov. 10, from around 13.4 million at the start of the month, Kpler data show. Recent data remain provisional as additional vessel crossings continue to be identified and validated. As producers boosted output last month, Saudi Arabia told the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries that the amount it actually supplied to the market was below its production. In the past, such a discrepancy has been an indication the kingdom was filling storage tanks or getting more out of Hormuz in advance of any escalation in the war. Both sides have lately stepped up tit-for-tat attacks in the ongoing war. US warplanes hit an Iranian missile launch site on Qeshm Island in the Persian Gulf this week, a response to Iran earlier targeting US personnel and assets. The chances of the US launching another round of mass strikes against Iran appear to have grown in recent days, according to Western officials, and the US issued a fresh warning to vessels breaching its blockade of Iranian ports this week. While the oil market has largely taken the recent flareups in its stride, that could change if attacks worsen. Abu Dhabi National Oil Co. said this week that one of its ships was hit when crossing Hormuz, that one seafarer was unaccounted for and a further 11 were injured. Kuwait has written to the IMO about attacks on eight of its tankers in recent weeks too. “Such actions undermine the security and stability of the region and constitute a clear breach of international law,” it said in a letter this week. “Kuwait reiterates its demands that the Islamic Republic of Iran immediately cease its unlawful attacks.” © 2026 Bloomberg L.P. articles.title: Panama Files Criminal Complaint Tied to CK Hutchison Ports Dispute
articles.summary: Panama's comptroller general said on Wednesday it had filed a criminal complaint over suspected irregularities uncovered in an audit of a state contract with a unit of Hong Kong conglomerate CK Hutchison.

REUTERS/Enea Lebrun PANAMA CITY, Nov 18 (Reuters) – Panama’s comptroller general said on Wednesday it had filed a criminal complaint over suspected irregularities uncovered in an audit of a state contract with a unit of Hong Kong conglomerate CK Hutchison . The comptroller’s office said the complaint seeks an investigation into possible crimes linked to the port concession contract between the state and the CK Hutchison unit, Panama Ports Company (PPC). It said the filing covers former board members of the Panama Maritime Authority between 2014 and 2023, former administrators of the authority during that period, and PPC itself. The authority and PPC did not immediately respond to requests for comment. The complaint stems from findings in an audit of the company’s financial statements and compliance with contractual obligations, the comptroller said. The office did not detail the suspected irregularities, but said it had turned over documentation to the public prosecutor for investigation. The move marks the latest development in a broader dispute over PPC’s role operating the Balboa and Cristobal ports near the Panama Canal, one of the world’s busiest maritime waterways. Earlier this year, Panama moved to unwind the company’s port concessions, escalating a legal and diplomatic fight involving PPC and CK Hutchison. PPC has also accused Panamanian authorities in recent months of unlawfully seizing property and documents during the takeover of the facilities, allegations President Jose Raul Mulino has rejected. The dispute has complicated CK Hutchison’s proposed sale of a majority stake in its global ports business to a consortium led by BlackRock and Mediterranean Shipping Company. Photo: Hanwha Philly Shipyard Hanwha Philly Shipyard has begun construction of the first of four medium-range (MR) oil and chemical tankers for Hanwha Shipping, marking the start of a new U.S.-built tanker program as the South Korean conglomerate expands its American shipbuilding operations. The Philadelphia shipyard held a steel-cutting ceremony on November 17, kicking off a multiyear construction program with vessel deliveries scheduled between 2029 and 2030. The four tankers, each approximately 49,500 deadweight tons, will be designed to transport crude oil, refined petroleum products and chemicals. The vessels will be built to comply with the Jones Act, which requires vessels carrying cargo between U.S. ports to be American-built, American-owned and American-crewed. According to Hanwha Philly Shipyard , the tankers will feature energy-efficient designs and meet International Maritime Organization Type 2 and Type 3 chemical tanker standards. An optional Type II configuration with 18 segregations will allow the vessels to carry different cargoes separately. The program represents the first construction of an MR tanker in the United States in nearly a decade, according to Hanwha Shipping. “At a time when the domestic tanker fleet continues to age, these vessels will help modernize U.S. maritime transportation and enhance the resilience of America’s energy supply chain,” said James Sagar, CEO of Hanwha Shipping. The project also provides another source of work for the Philadelphia yard, which Hanwha acquired in December 2024 as part of its broader push into the U.S. maritime and defense markets. The shipyard is already building commercial containerships for Matson and completing the National Security Multi-Mission Vessel program for the U.S. Maritime Administration. Hanwha Defense USA was also recently selected by TOTE Services to build a Medium Landing Ship for the U.S. Navy, expanding the yard’s work into naval shipbuilding . “A strong shipbuilding industry depends on consistent production, skilled people, and the ability to deliver quality vessels to our customers,” said Hyuk Kim, president of Hanwha Philly Shipyard. “This four-vessel program provides an important foundation for that work.” The tanker order strengthens Hanwha’s position in the domestic maritime market, adding new commercial construction work alongside its growing U.S. government shipbuilding portfolio. articles.summary: British marine accident investigators are calling for changes to superyacht safety regulations after the sinking of the luxury sailing yacht Bayesian exposed gaps in vessel stability standards, liferaft requirements and...

(Image: UK Marine Accident Investigation Branch) British marine accident investigators are calling for changes to superyacht safety regulations after the sinking of the luxury sailing yacht Bayesian exposed gaps in vessel stability standards, liferaft requirements and crew training that could put other large sailing yachts at risk. The recommendations, contained in the UK Marine Accident Investigation Branch’s (MAIB) final report released Thursday , follow the August 2024 disaster off Sicily that killed seven people, including British technology entrepreneur Mike Lynch and his daughter. While investigators found that Bayesian had an unrecognized vulnerability to extreme winds , the report goes further, identifying shortcomings in the regulatory framework governing large sailing yachts and recommending changes aimed at preventing similar accidents. At the center of the findings is a gap in the standards used to assess yacht stability. Neither the Large Commercial Yacht Code (LY2), under which Bayesian was built, nor the subsequent Red Ensign Group Yacht Code required certain monohull sailing yachts to be assessed for the risk of being knocked onto their sides by high winds when operating without sails. Investigators found that the yacht’s towering mast and furled sails still generated substantial wind forces, even while the vessel was anchored. However, its approved stability information did not account for that risk, leaving the crew unaware of a potentially catastrophic vulnerability. The MAIB has recommended that the Red Ensign Group study the vulnerability of monohull sailing yachts certified under its Yacht Code and amend the regulations based on its findings. It also wants improved stability information and operational guidance for crews preparing for extreme weather, whether underway or at anchor. The investigation identified another significant safety concern involving lifesaving equipment. None of Bayesian ‘s liferafts automatically floated free and inflated when the yacht sank. Although their hydrostatic release units operated, the rafts remained trapped by their stowage arrangements. A crew member was forced to manually release one, allowing the 15 survivors to remain afloat until they were rescued. Investigators found that the liferaft arrangements met the regulatory requirements applicable when the yacht was originally surveyed. However, those standards did not adequately address what happens when a large sailing yacht is knocked onto its side. The MAIB is now recommending amendments to the Red Ensign Group Yacht Code requiring liferafts aboard sailing vessels vulnerable to knockdown to be capable of floating free, inflating and separating from the vessel as it sinks. The report also identified a separate deficiency in Bayesian ‘s original stability approval. Investigators determined that the yacht did not meet LY2’s minimum downflooding-angle requirement, leaving it vulnerable to progressive flooding at lower heel angles than the code permitted. The MAIB classified that finding as a safety issue that did not directly contribute to the accident. Beyond vessel design, investigators are calling for improvements in marine weather forecasting and professional training. Thunderstorms had been forecast near the yacht’s anchorage, but the available warnings did not adequately communicate the potential for destructive downbursts. Within just 14 minutes, relatively calm conditions gave way to winds of at least 68 knots, knocking the yacht onto its side in less than 15 seconds. The MAIB has recommended that the UK’s Maritime and Coastguard Agency review yacht officer training requirements to better address thunderstorms, downbursts and extreme wind gusts. It has also urged the Met Office to raise the treatment of rare but potentially catastrophic weather events with the World Meteorological Organization, while calling for updated guidance in Admiralty nautical publications. In a separate safety flyer issued to the yachting industry , the MAIB urged yacht owners, managers and crews to examine their vessels’ vulnerability to extreme weather and ensure their operating procedures adequately address the risks. “Our investigation found that Bayesian had a vulnerability to high winds that was not recognised,” said Rob Loder, the UK’s Chief Inspector of Marine Accidents. Loder urged regulators, training providers and weather services to act on the investigation’s recommendations to prevent another tragedy. The proposed changes are not yet binding regulations. According to the final report, no safety actions had been taken by other organizations at the time of publication. The MAIB has also prepared a paper detailing the hazards identified in the investigation for consideration by the International Maritime Organization’s Sub-Committee on Implementation of IMO Instruments, potentially extending the safety discussion beyond the superyacht sector. articles.title: $960 million deal enabling NEO NEXT+ to bring EnQuest’s UK North Sea business into its fold
articles.summary: London Stock Exchange-listed energy firm EnQuest has decided to exit the UK upstream arena to strengthen its focus on Southeast Asia.
articles.body: Business & Finance November 19, 2026 · 6 minutes ago $960 million deal enabling NEO NEXT+ to bring EnQuest’s UK North Sea business into its fold London Stock Exchange-listed energy firm EnQuest has decided to exit the UK upstream arena to strengthen its focus on Southeast Asia. MC Melisa Cavcic Senior Editor 4 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Magnus platform Source: EnQuest UK’s independent oil and gas producer NEO NEXT+ Energy is boosting its portfolio with the acquisition of EnQuest’s UK upstream business and associated infrastructure, as the seller accelerates its pivot toward Southeast Asia, following a series of acquisitions in Malaysia. EnQuest has entered into an agreement to sell its UK upstream business and associated infrastructure through the sale of EnQuest Britain to NEO NEXT+ Energy for total consideration of up to $960 million, encompassing $840 million in upfront cash consideration to be paid on completion, subject to customary closing adjustments, including working capital, together with up to $120 million contingent cash consideration. The proposed disposal is based on an economic effective date of January 1, 2027, and is subject to customary conditions, including, among others, regulatory approvals and completion of the firm’s acquisitions of participating interests in four PSCs in Malaysia, which remain on track to complete on December 31, 2026. These moves continue EnQuest’s strategic pivot to Southeast Asia as its primary operating region, creating a low-cost, highly resilient platform from which to pursue further near-term capital-efficient organic and inorganic growth. Following completion of the proposed disposal, EnQuest intends to repay debt drawn in connection with the proposed acquisitions, while retaining significant liquidity and financial flexibility to pursue material organic growth and further acquisition opportunities across the region. Related Articles Fossil Energy EnQuest makes $833 million play to expand its Southeast Asian oil & gas arsenal 3 min read " The resulting business will have a materially lower cost base and significantly enhanced balance sheet strength to pursue both organic investment and further value-accretive acquisitions across Southeast Asia, while supporting sustainable shareholder returns. We are immensely proud of what our teams have achieved in the UK and believe that NEO NEXT+’s combination of scale and track record as a leading North Sea operator, and diverse asset portfolio will enhance career opportunities for our people. We are committed to working closely with NEO NEXT+, our employees, joint venture partners and other stakeholders to ensure an orderly transition. " — Amjad Bseisu Chief Executive Officer of EnQuest The company’s board of directors believes the proposed disposal represents a significant step forward in the continued strategic evolution of EnQuest, crystallizing material value from the firm’s UK upstream portfolio, significantly strengthening its capital structure and completing the repositioning toward Southeast Asia. EnQuest took these steps to establish Southeast Asia as its primary operating region, where it sees significant opportunities for further high-return, capital-efficient growth, and maintain its established focus on operatorship and highly tangible reserves, deploying its operating capabilities and experienced asset teams to enhance value via a number of measures, including recovery factor improvement and conversion of 2C resources. In addition, the company believes this divestment and recent acquisitions provide a strengthened platform from which to accelerate further organic growth initiatives in Southeast Asia and capitalize on further inorganic growth opportunities across the region. The remaining EnQuest portfolio on a 2025 net participating interest basis, following completion of the proposed disposal and the acquisitions, is expected to benefit from around 70,000 barrels of oil equivalent per day (boe/d) in the Southeast Asia business, with a unit opex of about $11/boe, a reduction of approximately 57% against its 2025 unit opex of $25/boe, generating a pro forma EBITDA of circa $500 million. While elaborating that production has grown further via the addition of low-cost Seligi 1b gas volumes in 2026, the firm emphasizes the substantial capital-efficient growth potential, including opportunities to leverage existing infrastructure, adding that its Southeast Asia capital investment is focused on high-return production enhancement activity, with minimal infrastructure investment required. The proposed disposal will involve the sale of all of the issued shares of EnQuest Britain, which through its subsidiaries holds the firm’s UK upstream assets, including Magnus , Kraken , and the Greater Kittiwake Area (operated), Golden Eagle (non-operated), and the undeveloped Bressay field and Bentley discovery. Additionally, the portfolio entails UK decommissioning and midstream assets, including EnQuest’s operating interest in the Sullom Voe Terminal , the Northern Leg Gas Pipeline , and the Ninian Pipeline system. Employees supporting these operations will transfer to the new owner as a result of the deal. EnQuest’s UK upstream assets contributed 31,122 boe/d of average net production (92% liquids and 8% gas) for the year ended December 31, 2025, when the portfolio comprised approximately 122 million boe of 2P reserves and 308 million boe of 2C resources. " The proposed disposal represents a significant repositioning of EnQuest, continuing the company’s transformation from a UK-focused operator into a business focused on high-quality assets in Southeast Asia, underpinned by a simple, strong capital structure. Following completion of both the proposed acquisitions and the proposed disposal, EnQuest will be a significant operator of scale, with its upstream portfolio focused solely on its 97% operated 2P asset base in Southeast Asia. " — EnQuest underlined. The completion of the divestment is expected in the first quarter of 2027, subject to conditions set out in the agreement, such as receipt of applicable regulatory approvals, including NSTA and NSIA approval and CMA clearance; completion of the company’s previously announced proposed acquisitions of participating interests offshore Malaysia; and other customary approvals and consents, including, amongst others, RBL lender consent and replacement of UK Decommissioning Security Agreements. Upon completion of the disposal, EnQuest will have interests in production, development, and exploration assets in Malaysia, Vietnam, Brunei, and Indonesia, as well as Veri Energy, a wholly owned subsidiary, and associated CCUS interests, which sit outside this perimeter.
